newsitem.title: USA: Dow adds Hewlett, Travelers, Wal-Mart to DJIA.
newsitem.headline: Dow adds Hewlett, Travelers, Wal-Mart to DJIA.

text.p: Dow Jones & Co Inc's Wall Street Journal said on Wednesday it would add Travelers Group Inc, Johnson & Johnson, Wal-Mart Stores Inc and Hewlett-Packard Co to the Dow Jones Industrial Average, effective March 17.
Travelers would replace Westinghouse Electric Corp, Hewlett would replace Texaco Inc, Johnson & Johnson would replace Bethlehem Steel Corp, and Wal-Mart would replace Woolworth Corp, Dow Jones said.
Changes in the components of the 30-stock average were decided by the editors of the Wall Street Journal, which is published by Dow Jones, the company said.

"We've always thought of 'industrials' as meaning more than manufacturing," said Paul Steiger, managing editor of The Wall Street Journal. "Nowadays, technological innovation and services of all types are major propellants of the U.S. economy."

Dow Jones said it decided to replace Westinghouse in the stock average after the company announced plans to spin off its industrial operations later. This would make Westinghouse, which owns the CBS television network, primarily a broadcasting company, Dow Jones noted.
Broadcasting was already well represented in the industrial average by General Electric Co, which owns NBC and Walt Disney Co, which owns American Broadcasting Co ABC, Dow Jones said.

Dow Jones said the addition of Travelers Group will expand the representation of financial services in the industrial average, Johnson & Johnson, a major pharmaceuticals company, added health-care representation, and Hewlett-Packard expanded technology representation.

The changes would cause the divisor used to calculate the average to rise slightly and the new level would be determined after the close of trading on the New York Stock Exchange on March 14, Dow Jones said.
The average was originally computed by adding the prices of the stocks and dividing by the number of stocks.
But to avoid the average being distorted by stock splits or substitutions, the divisor is now changed with each alteration to preserve historical continuity, it said.

The most recent changes in the industrial average were made in May 1991, when Caterpillar Inc, Walt Disney Co and J.P. Morgan & Co Inc were substituted for Navistar International Corp, USX-US Steel Group and Primerica Corp, the company said.
Primerica subsequently bought insurance company Travelers and changed its name to Travelers Group, the company said.

"It's intentional that we don't change the stocks often," said John Prestbo, markets editor of the Journal. "The Dow Jones Industrial Average isn't a 'hot stock' index, after all, and we believe that stability of composition enhances the trust that many people have in the industrial average."

The change in components of the industrial average would also require a change in the divisor used to calculate the related composite index of 65 stocks, which also included the 20-stock transportation and the 15-stock utilities averages.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average marked its hundredth anniversary in 1996, but its roots trace to July 3, 1884, when Charles Dow, a co-founder of Dow Jones, produced a stock market average of 11 stocks, nine of which were railroad issues. On May 26, 1896, the Dow Jones Industrial Average, comprised of 12 stocks, made its debut.
Later other stocks were added, and the first publication of an average comparable to today's 30 industrial stocks was October 1, 1928, the company said.
